messages.author: 222cf5fedef64b1e
messages.subject: longitudinal CFA
parts:
Dear list members,

I am trying to accomplish a confirmatory factor analysis of a rating scale, assessing measurement invariance across three assessments.

I thought that by using the lavaan.survey package I'd be able to account for dependence among observations. However, thus far I have only managed to produce fit statistics for configural and weak invariance, but not been able to compare these two.

I would appreciate any info on how to get tests of incremental fit.

I'm a rather novice R user (changed from AMOS because of R's versatility) and hope that there is a simple solution.

Regards,

Filip


My model: Three correlated factors with 5, 8, and 7 indicators, respectively. The error variance is set free for two indicators in one factor.
N=1350 with complete data.

#config invariance
mod1fit <- cfa(mod1, dataLong, estimator="MLM", group="time")
survey.design<-svydesign(ids=~id, data=dataLong)
survey.fit<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=mod1fit, survey.design=survey.design)

#weak invariance
mod2fit <- cfa(mod1, dataLong, estimator="MLM", group="time", group.equal="loadings")
survey.fit2<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=mod2fit, survey.design=survey.design)

On 11/29/2013 11:53 PM, Filip Arnberg wrote:
> Dear list members,
>
> I am trying to accomplish a confirmatory factor analysis of a rating
> scale, assessing measurement invariance across three assessments.
>
> I thought that by using the lavaan.survey package I'd be able to account
> for dependence among observations. However, thus far I have only managed
> to produce fit statistics for configural and weak invariance, but not
> been able to compare these two.

I think you are looking for the anova() function, which can be used to
compare two nested models:

anova(survey.fit, survey.fit2)

If the p-value is NOT significant, you have established (weak) invariance.

Yves.

On 12/03/2013 10:02 AM, Filip Arnberg wrote:
Hi, please see attached for a data snippet and the R script.

Thanks. I found the problem, although I'm not sure how I can solve it. Objects returned by the lavaan.survey() do not include the raw data anymore (in the slot @Data@X). And the anova() function needs the raw data if the test statistics are scaled.

As a workaround, you can use the 'hidden' option SB.classic=TRUE:

> anova(survey.fit,survey.fit2, SB.classic=TRUE)

survey.fit  615 30644 31567 1125.1
survey.fit2 653 30641 31397 1160.7     38.587      38      0.443

Yves.

Hi list,

Just a comment on chi-square difference testing using survey data: using the raw data and scaled test statistics, it would not come out right if there were weights. There is no literature on this as far as I know (but I would greatly enjoy being corrected!). 

So SB.classic (Satorra-Bentler chisq difference testing) is indeed the best way to go the literature has to offer right now..

Best, Daniel

messages.author: 949f9be37ba0e6cd
messages.subject: Re: longitudinal CFA
parts:
Closer to (a) though it is not that bad.

All of these statistics are approximations: SB matches the mean of the distribution, while other statistics also match the variance. The issue of difference testing is then also different for these two types of statistics. You need these in the situation of complex sampling using pseudo-ML but also (more famously) when there is nonnormality and you fit using ML (in fact this is also pseudo-ML). There are very few simulations, however, specifically using complex survey data rather than nonnormality (some were done by Asparouhov & Muthén).

What I think nobody has done yet is 1) describe exactly how you would deal with sample weights when calculating some of these variance adjusted difference tests, though this should not be too difficult to work out;  and 2) simulated chi-square _difference testing_  under complex sampling to evaluate the different approaches. 

On the other hand, quite a bit of work has been done on this issue in the context of nonnormality, from which we know that SB difference testing often works well. That is why I say it is not as bad as knowing nothing.
